item.title: “Having gone forth, Anuruddhas, what should a clansman do? Anuruddhas, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states. If he does not attain…
item.description:
“Having gone forth, Anuruddhas, what should a clansman do? Anuruddhas, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states. If he does not attain rapture and pleasure or some other state more peaceful than that, then sensual lust invades his mind and remains; ill-will … sloth and torpor … restlessness and remorse … doubt … discontent … laziness invades his mind and remains. Anuruddhas, when he has not secluded himself from sensual desires, from unwholesome states, he does not attain rapture and pleasure or some other state more peaceful than that. Anuruddhas, when he does seclude himself from sensual desires, from unwholesome states, he attains rapture and pleasure or some other state more peaceful than that; then sensual lust does not invade his mind and remain; ill-will … sloth and torpor … restlessness and remorse … doubt … discontent … laziness does not invade his mind and remain. Anuruddhas, when he has secluded himself from sensual desires, from unwholesome states, he attains rapture and pleasure or some other state more peaceful than that.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 68 – Naḷakapānasutta

item.title: Elder Uttiya: “Hearing a sound, mindfulness is lost — Attending to a pleasing sign, The mind feels infatuation, Clinging to the perception remains. The defilements…
item.description:
Elder Uttiya:
“Hearing a sound, mindfulness is lost —
Attending to a pleasing sign,
The mind feels infatuation,
Clinging to the perception remains.
The defilements increase,
Leading to defilement in saṃsāra.”

From: Theragāthā 1.99

item.title: Behold this decorated image — A heap of wounds, a collection of sores, Diseased, the object of many lustful thoughts, Nothing stable or permanent here.…
item.description:
Behold this decorated image —
A heap of wounds, a collection of sores,
Diseased, the object of many lustful thoughts,
Nothing stable or permanent here.

Behold this adorned appearance,
With jewels and earrings,
A skeleton covered by skin,
Made beautiful by clothes.

The feet are painted with lac and dye,
The face is smeared with powder and paste —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

The hair is curled in seven rings,
The eyes are rubbed with collyrium and rouge —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

Like a newly decorated medicine box,
This foul body is adorned for the occasion —
Enough to fool a fool,
But not one who seeks the far shore.

The hunter set his trap and snare,
The wise deer does not approach,
Having eaten the crops, we go our way,
Leaving the trapper to lament.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 82 – Raṭṭhapālasutta

item.title: - “Venerable sir, right view — for what purpose is it?” - “Right view, Rādha, is for the purpose of disenchantment.” - “Venerable sir, disenchantment…
item.description:
- “Venerable sir, right view — for what purpose is it?” - “Right view, Rādha, is for the purpose of disenchantment.” - “Venerable sir, disenchantment — for what purpose is it?” - “Disenchantment, Rādha, is for the purpose of dispassion.” - “Venerable sir, dispassion — for what purpose is it?” - “Dispassion, Rādha, is for the purpose of liberation.” - “Venerable sir, liberation — for what purpose is it?” - “Liberation, Rādha, is for the purpose of Nibbāna.” - “Venerable sir, Nibbāna — for what purpose is it?” - “Rādha, you have gone beyond the range of this question. For the purpose of entering Nibbāna, Rādha, is the holy life lived; Nibbāna is its final goal, Nibbāna is its end.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 23.1

item.title: “Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and saw beings with little dust in their…
item.description:
“Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties and with dull faculties, with good dispositions and with bad dispositions, some easy to teach and some hard to teach, and a few who saw the danger in rebirth in another world and the danger of faulty actions. Just as in a blue lotus pond, a red lotus pond, or a white lotus pond, some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, do not rise above the water, and are nourished underwater; some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and reach the water’s surface; some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, rise up above the water and are not wetted by the water.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 14 – Mahāpadānasutta

item.title: “Monk, cultivate seclusion, Do not be heedless, Do not let your mind whirl in sensual pleasures. If you are heedless, you will swallow a hot…
item.description:
“Monk, cultivate seclusion,
Do not be heedless,
Do not let your mind whirl in sensual pleasures.
If you are heedless, you will swallow a hot iron ball,
And when burned, do not cry out in pain!”

“Without wisdom, there is no jhāna;
Without jhāna, there is no wisdom.
One who has both jhāna and wisdom
Is indeed close to Nibbāna.”

“Entering an empty house,
A monk with a peaceful mind
Experiences a superhuman delight
In the clear vision of the Dhamma.”

“When he clearly comprehends
The arising and passing away of the aggregates,
He gains joy and rapture —
That is the deathless for those who know.”

From: Dhammapada 360-382

item.title: “‘How, monks, should a monk contemplate so that his consciousness is not distracted or scattered externally, and does not abide internally, and is not agitated…
item.description:
“‘How, monks, should a monk contemplate so that his consciousness is not distracted or scattered externally, and does not abide internally, and is not agitated by clinging? If his consciousness is not distracted or scattered externally, does not abide internally, and is not agitated by clinging, then there is no arising, origination of suffering regarding future birth, aging, and death.’ Good sirs, how is consciousness distracted and scattered externally? Here, good sirs, when a monk sees a form with the eye, consciousness pursues the sign of form, is tied to the enjoyment of the sign of form, is bound by the fetter of the enjoyment of the sign of form—this is called consciousness distracted and scattered externally. When he hears a sound with the ear … smells an odor with the nose … tastes a flavor with the tongue … feels a touch with the body … cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, consciousness pursues the sign of phenomenon, is tied to the enjoyment of the sign of phenomenon, is bound by the fetter of the enjoyment of the sign of phenomenon—this is called consciousness distracted and scattered externally. Thus, good sirs, is consciousness distracted and scattered externally.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 138 – Uddesavibhaṅgasutta

item.title: “Householder, suppose a vulture, a kite, or a hawk seizes a piece of meat and flies up. Then other vultures, kites, or hawks chase after…
item.description:
“Householder, suppose a vulture, a kite, or a hawk seizes a piece of meat and flies up. Then other vultures, kites, or hawks chase after it, attacking and tearing at that piece of meat. What do you think, householder? If that vulture, kite, or hawk does not quickly let go of that piece of meat, would it thereby meet death or deadly suffering?” “Yes, venerable sir.” … “So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat — of much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater.’ Having seen this as it actually is with perfect wisdom, having abandoned the equanimity based on diversity … he cultivates such equanimity.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 54 – Potaliyasutta

item.title: - Who ages, who does not age? What is called the wrong path? What is an obstacle to the Dhamma? What destroys day and night?…
item.description:
- Who ages, who does not age?
What is called the wrong path?
What is an obstacle to the Dhamma?
What destroys day and night?
What defiles the holy life?
What is a bath without water?
How many openings in the world
Upon which the mind does not dwell?
I have come to ask the Blessed One —
Please tell me the answers!
- Form in beings ages,
The name-nature does not age,
Greed is called the wrong path,
Craving is an obstacle to the Dhamma.
Aging destroys day and night,
Women defile the holy life —
Ensnared in this defilement
Are all beings.
Austerities and the holy life
Are a bath without water.
There are six openings in the world
Upon which the mind does not dwell:
Laziness and heedlessness,
Lethargy and lack of self-control,
Drowsiness and sloth —
These six openings should be
Completely abandoned.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.76

item.title: “Monks, there are these two kinds of pleasure. What two? Sensual pleasure and the pleasure of renunciation. These, monks, are the two pleasures. The best…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these two kinds of pleasure. What two? Sensual pleasure and the pleasure of renunciation. These, monks, are the two pleasures. The best of these two pleasures, monks, is the pleasure of renunciation.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 2.65
